vignette:
Kareem Mansouri is a 48-year-old divorced Middle Eastern man who works as a fashion designer in New York City. He was referred for psychological assessment following a brief contact with his primary care physician, to whom he had gone for persistent gastrointestinal complaints. What emerged in that appointment, haltingly and with evident reluctance, was a picture that had been forming for nearly two years - one that Kareem himself had been working hard not to look at directly.

Approximately twenty-two months ago, Kareem was present at a large commercial building fire in the garment district, a blaze that broke out during a trade showcase he was attending with several colleagues. The fire spread with a speed that the building's layout seemed designed to trap: stairwells filled with black smoke, emergency lighting failed on the lower floors, and for a period that Kareem estimates at around fifteen minutes - though he acknowledges he cannot be certain - he was pressed into a crowd of people in a corridor that grew unbearably, suffocatingly hot. The heat was not the ambient warmth of a summer afternoon but something pressing and invasive, a specific quality of air against the back of his neck and forearms that felt almost deliberate. He tasted smoke so thickly that it coated his mouth. One of his colleagues collapsed beside him. Kareem eventually reached an exit, but the colleague did not survive.

In the weeks that followed, Kareem noticed that his recollection of the event did not behave like other memories. It did not sit in the past. It arrived without warning - a fragment of the corridor, the sound of alarms, the texture of the wall he pressed his palm against - and when it came, it did not feel remembered so much as re-entered. He would be standing at his cutting table and the memory would arrive mid-motion, and for a moment the studio would cease to exist. The taste of smoke returned with these intrusions, coating his mouth as freshly as it had that evening, and he would find himself gripping the table's edge as nausea moved through him. What disturbed him most was that the pieces never assembled into a coherent whole. He could not tell the story of that night from beginning to end. He had fragments - the heat on his neck, a particular scream, the colleague's face - but they did not connect, and he had come to believe that somewhere in the gaps was something he was not yet able to know.

Kareem began, without quite deciding to, restructuring his life around what felt safest. He could not enter any space - a restaurant, a client's showroom, a subway car - without first identifying where the exits were. He would pause at the entrance, locate them, trace the route mentally, and only then allow himself to move further inside. He scanned every room he entered with a vigilance he recognised as excessive but could not relinquish. His concentration at work, which had always been one of his professional strengths, became unreliable; he would lose the thread of a design meeting and return to find his colleagues watching him. Over time, two junior designers he had mentored for years quietly transferred to other studios. He was certain this was because his erratic presence had made the work environment unstable, and he said nothing to stop them.

At home, he checked the locks on his apartment door multiple times before bed - sometimes returning from the hallway after having already left - and on nights when the intrusions were worst, he had hurt himself physically, pressing something sharp against his forearm, a behaviour he disclosed to his physician with shame and described as the only thing that returned him to the present moment. He had also thrown himself into his work with an intensity that his ex-wife, with whom he remained in cautious contact, described as frightening. He worked until two or three in the morning, filling every quiet hour.

What finally brought him to seek help was a fitting appointment last month in which a client's heated studio - warm in the particular way the corridor had been warm - sent him out of the room without explanation. He stood on the pavement for ten minutes, unable to re-enter. He told his physician he was afraid there was nothing left of the person he had been before that night, and he was hoping, with considerable doubt, to be proven wrong.
